title: Christ Formed in Us Through Faith and Ascetic Discipline
english: My children, I am again in the pains of labor for you until Christ is inwardly formed in your souls.
This formation of Christ within you happens in no other way than through a faith without reproach and a way of life shaped by the gospel.
For we do not walk by the outward oldness of the written code, but by the inward newness that comes from the Spirit, especially those of you who are making your way toward God.

I believe this also works effectively within us when we prepare our minds for every good deed, stretching them taut like nerves, so that our very thoughts may become pure and undistorted, not monstrous or warped.

In this state we willingly accept this most blessed fast, observing it with measured moderation in our eating, free from useless curiosity about what we may eat, and keeping our partaking of food simple and undistracted, so that we may also sharpen the eye of our understanding.
Yet we know well that the toil of the flesh alone does not bring holiness to our souls, nor does mere abstinence suffice to display true virtue before others.
True holiness requires the purity that comes from righteous actions joined with the dignity of a holy life, and it is sustained by the joyful witness of those who truly accomplish the fast.
Therefore I maintain, and indeed I say more strongly, that what is most necessary is to give ourselves completely and wholly to the worship of Christ, holding nothing back from that devotion.

Let us not turn away in any direction from the straight path, abandoning the firm way by which one walks toward God, to be carried off course instead, and let us not foolishly complete our end in what appears to the devil as reasonable, for as the Savior himself said, no one is able to serve two masters.
For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other.
Therefore, we must reject the non-existing master, I mean Satan, so that we may truly love the Lord who truly exists.
What manner of love's conduct will arise among us? He himself will lead by his own example, saying the Lord: 'The one who loves me keeps my commandments.' (John 14:15)
And those who are genuine guardians of the Savior's command possess piety, and do not endure the greed of the devil, but they shake off the yoke of sin and look toward a free disposition.
Crushing every foreign and hateful pleasure, and mortifying the desires of the flesh by the labors of asceticism.
And even he himself crying out, you will hear Paul: 'For those of Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.' (Galatians 5:24)

Therefore, I will say again, taking from Paul: 'If we live by the Spirit, we also walk by the Spirit, mortifying the members that are upon the earth, namely fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed.' (Galatians 5:16-25)
Presenting ourselves rather as a fragrance of sweet smell, according to what is written, and setting up a spiritual sacrifice, as it were, we give life to the God who loves virtue.
For the fruit of the labors of the good will always be glorious.
Do not let anyone among us think that he will achieve the good without effort, having come to trial without any sweat, and will boast in the sin.
For the most savage tyrant of the Egyptians laid upon them a hard yoke of slavery, never ceasing in his labors, reducing the Jews to making mud and bricks.

But God, having pity on them, saw how they were worn out and exhausted by their ruler’s inhumanity, and considered how to bring them back from above and restore their most ancient freedom; thus he commanded Moses, the all-wise, to say that he was going forth from among the Egyptians, the tyrant.
‘Thus says the Lord God of the Hebrews: Send forth my people, that they may serve me in the wilderness.’ (Exodus 5:1)
Why then did he not rather command them to serve in Egypt? And why did he call them to desert places?

Is it not reasonable to perceive that those who were about to serve the God who rules over all first thought it necessary to send away the yoke of another’s slavery, and then to discard, as one does with the commands of demons, what must be done under compulsion, and to cease also from mud and brick-making?

title: Purification and Redemption
english: To achieve purification from earthly impurities, it is necessary to escape the grasp of those who have taken advantage of us, so that we might approach the services to God in purity, being pure and acting purely.
The great Moses was calling the Israelites to do this when he led them to the pure desert, away from the corrupting influences of Egypt.
However, Pharaoh was puffed up and trampled on the divine glory, refusing to acknowledge the Lord and insisting that he would not let the Israelites go.
As Pharaoh was being conquered by the blows from above, he became increasingly unwilling to let the Israelites go, and his whole land was in danger, ultimately leading to his downfall.

In his attempts to hinder the Israelites, Pharaoh devised various ways to keep them in slavery, saying that they could go and sacrifice to the Lord their God in his land, but this was just another ploy to keep them under his control and prevent them from truly serving God.
We see how even when the law of God leads us out of sin, Satan rises up in opposition.
Our Savior Jesus Christ, who has surpassed all life, is involuntarily dragging away greed, not having a field for a cavalry.
But he does not allow us to be completely outside of our own land; instead, we are to share, as he commands, both in what seems good to him and in what is pleasing to the Master of all.

Ultimately, it is impossible for us to have a blameless way of service unless we have completely gone out of the devil's land and are found to be completely without a share in his slavery, having been set free by Christ.
Moses said to Pharaoh, 'Go, sacrifice to the Lord your God in my land,' which implies that it is not possible to serve two masters.
This is because no one can simultaneously fulfill the demands of two conflicting authorities, and we must choose to serve either God or the devil.
The Israelites, having been enslaved in Egypt, had to throw off the yoke of their oppressors and overcome the hand of those who formerly prevailed, trusting in God's power to deliver them.

They were able to do so because they had sacrificed the lamb in Egypt as a type of Christ, and had been anointed with the blood, and had eaten unleavened bread on it, foreshadowing the redemption that would come through Christ.
Our souls must be fortified through the truest and most mystical blessing, if we renounce serving sins and instead choose to follow God's will.
The only way to escape the overwhelming power of earthly passions is through our participation in Christ, which enables us to weaken the power of Satan.
This is why Christ, who is God by nature and the Only-Begotten of God the Father, voluntarily came down to emptiness, taking on the form of a servant.
He did this to elevate the lowliness of our human nature to great heights, granting it the security that it lacks.

By mingling Himself with our nature, which is prone to evil, Christ gave us the security of His own unchangeable nature, so that our minds might be firmly established in good works and our flesh might be transformed.
As a result, the passions of our flesh are completely mortified by the power of the indwelling God, the Word.
Paul conveys to us a message of hope and transformation through our participation in Christ.

God sent his own Son in a body like ours, prone to sin, and condemned sin in that body, so that the law's demands might be fully met in us who do not live according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

As a result, sin has been condemned and put to death, first in Christ and eventually in us, when we allow him to dwell in our hearts through faith and the Spirit's presence, transforming us into his likeness through the power of holiness.
The Spirit of our Savior Christ is, in a sense, a reflection of him, bearing the image of our divine nature.
Jesus said, 'I am the truth' (John 14:6), and John wrote, 'The Spirit is the truth' (1 John 5:6).
Paul said, 'The Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom' (2 Corinthians 3:17).
The mystagogue has preserved the unity of the Son and the Holy Spirit, both in substance and in distinct conception, according to what is said to exist, which each is said to be and truly is.

The Spirit is reasonably considered to be the Spirit, and not the Son, but rather the Spirit of the Son, forming and transforming into itself the things in which it participates, so that God and the Father, seeing the characters of his own offspring in us, may love us as children and honor us with heavenly honors.
Moses said, 'Sanctify to me every firstborn, every firstborn that opens the womb' (Exodus 13:2), meaning that these firstborns should be registered and dedicated as holy and indebted to God.

The law of God and the Father shows his eternal will by taking the spiritual likeness as a type, as Moses spoke to the sons of Israel, saying that if the Lord their God brings them into the land of the Canaanites, they should destroy every male that opens the womb and dedicate it to the Lord.
For all who are holy, wherever the image of the holy and firstborn Christ shines forth, are sanctified, set apart for God's service and conformed to the image of His Son.

Paul says that for those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, and those whom he predestined, he also called, and those whom he called, he also justified, and those whom he justified, he also glorified (Romans 8:29-30).
The transcendent beauty, which is thought to be on the divine and supernatural substance, is the one that transforms us, conforming us to the image of Christ.

As the character is revealed in our souls, if we are partakers of the divine nature, having received the Spirit of the Father and the Son, we are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as from the Lord Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:18).

In deeds and in the power of virtue, the transformation and transfiguration in us take place, towards whatever is pleasing to God, and casting out all weakness of our mind, and transforming it into a firm and invincible phronema.
The law shows us the way to achieve this transformation, and it is through our participation in Christ that we can overcome the power of sin and be conformed to the image of God's Son.

title: Masculine and Feminine Principles
english: God, the giver, does not simply sanctify every firstborn, but rather adds that the male is suitable. For the female, even if it is firstborn, is not sanctified unless it is said again at the right time and need. The male and youthful aspect is seen in the divine and incomprehensible nature, which is always masculine in generation. This nature of divinity is unconquerable and victorious, and it is this aspect that is reflected in Christ, who is thought to be symmetrical if he is somehow masculine and youthful in all good things.

In contrast, the female is not such, but rather soft and easily persuaded. The female gender is weak and inactive, and unaccustomed to battle and courage. An image of this is given from the writings of Moses, where the tyrant of the Egyptians, a type of the devil, armed himself against the pain of the Hebrews and ordered the newborns to be killed, and the male was to be drowned in the waters and marshes.

The devil takes great pleasure in thoughts that are soft, unmanly, and effeminate. He allows the female to grow, not expecting to be surpassed by them, for he considers the male to be most hostile and hard to conquer. The one who is nourished on the words of truth, if he reaches the measure of age in Christ and will grow into a perfect man, according to Paul (Romans 16:5), will not be captured, for he takes away before maturity. What is precious to God is detestable to him, and he will certainly prevail over the opposite.

The devil casts a vote, as it were, the best one, for himself, rejecting the devil's slander with the rest of his good order. This is evident from the holy Scriptures. In the book of Numbers (Numbers 1:2), God says to Moses and Aaron, 'Take a census of the whole congregation of the sons of Israel, by families, by fathers' houses, by number, by name, by head.'

The Lord commands that every male from twenty years and above, who goes out in the power of Israel, should be inspected. The female, on the other hand, is completely excluded from this command, and the youthful age is also not included. This is because the weak and immature mindset is rejected by God.

The manly and intelligent individual is well-known, even in the book of life, and is able to resist the devil's evil deeds. This is because the youthful mindset, combined with intelligence, is sufficient for all the things that pertain to the devout. As the Spirit makes us conformed to Christ, the divine characters shine forth in us through the energy of virtue. However, the opposite will happen to those who are not such. The power of the word will be made clear, as we see how the male is taken as a type of courage, and the female is introduced as a type of softness and weak mindset, which easily falls into pleasures. The divine Scripture itself shapes sin and the workers of sin in the form of the female.

The most unseemly shape of sin is deeply ingrained in the souls of those who love sin. To illustrate this, I will present the prophet Zechariah, who explains this concept clearly to those who listen. According to Zechariah, an angel spoke to him, showing him a vision of a measuring container with a woman sitting inside, representing wickedness. This vision illustrates the souls that try to elevate wickedness, having the same tendency towards evil, and being prone to uncleanness and fleshly desires.

The prophet's description of the two women with wings like a stork, lifting the container, is particularly noteworthy. The stork, a bird that feeds on unclean things, is a fitting symbol for the unclean and fleshly desires that characterize the souls that love sin.

The pure mind is nourished by the words of truth, and this truth is none other than Christ Himself. In contrast, the earthly and filthy mind gathers and feeds on the foul desires that arise within it, completely disregarding the resulting stench. If we consider it a pleasant and dear thing to bear the most glorious image of the Savior and to be transformed towards that divine and heavenly beauty, then we must reject the disgusting character of sin.

We must flee the soft and indulgent mind, which is easily swayed by the devil's wickedness, and instead become masculine and courageous in Christ. For it is through Him that we become partakers of His life, having become in the face of God and the Father. In this way, we will cast off the corruption that has taken up residence in our bodies, as if shedding one of the most burdensome loads, and we will put on the glory of righteousness, not denying the nature of the flesh, but being transformed into the glory of incorruptibility, and with our flesh and in some ineffable way, shining with the glory that comes from Christ. For it is written, 'He will transform our body of humiliation to be conformed to His glorious body' (Philippians 3:21).

God, who is all-powerful, wanted to teach us that even things that are perishable by nature can be transformed into something else and made better, if they are worthy of his care. This is evident in the fact that the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, as it is written in the Psalms (Psalm 34:15). In the book of Numbers, God speaks to Moses and Aaron, instructing them to fill a golden jar with manna, which would be preserved for their generations. Moses then tells Aaron, 'Take a golden urn and put the full manna in it and place it before God for preservation for your generations' (Numbers 11:5). Although the manna was perishable and useless for those who wanted to keep it, only lasting for one day, it remained imperishable when placed before God through Aaron's hand and connected with the golden urn.
